lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Traveling is the best way to learn! Skye flies with us part of the way, then waves goodbye. We walk with Ms. Emma into a town called Willowford. Look! There's a big old building with a round green roof and wide stone steps. It's the Hall of Wisdom! Inside, there is a round meeting hall with seats in a circle. A barn owl with round glasses flies down, holding a small wooden bell. Ding! She says, Welcome! I'm Olive, the chairperson of the Children's Council. Every voice matters! Birimo whispers, What is a council? Ms. Emma says, It's a group that meets to share ideas and decide things together. Olive says, Children from many places meet here to talk. Say it with me. Children from many places meet here to talk. Wonderful! In the center, an old tree grows indoors with six empty branches. Olive says, This is the Tree of Voices. When children share ideas kindly and listen well, a golden leaf grows. Let's read the sign by the door. "Welcome to the Hall of Wisdom! Here, children from many places meet to talk about things that matter to them. At the Children's Council, everyone can speak, and everyone listens. You may agree, or you may disagree, but please be kind. Raise your hand when you want to speak, and wait for your turn. Remember, good listeners make good speakers. Every voice matters!" When do you raise your hand? When you want to speak. Who makes a good speaker? A good listener. Then we meet three new friends. Leo is from a mountain town and loves soccer. Amara is from a seaside village and loves animals. Priya is from a big city and loves books. Now, phonics. Ity makes a noun. Equal becomes equality. Diverse, drop the e, becomes diversity. Curious changes ous to os: curiosity. Say the part before ity strongly. e-QUAL-i-ty, di-VER-si-ty, cu-ri-OS-i-ty. Next time, the council talks about school uniforms!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Children from many places meet here to talk. This morning, twenty council children sit in the big circle. We sit with Ms. Emma, and Birimo is so excited that he can't stop wiggling. Olive rings her little wooden bell. Ding! She says, Good morning, everyone! Here is our first question. Should students wear uniforms? Say it with me. Should students wear uniforms? Great! Olive says, There is no wrong answer. Let's listen to both sides. Leo raises his hand first. Then Priya raises her hand. Let's read what they said. "Leo says: At my school, we all wear uniforms. I think uniforms are good because everyone looks the same, so nobody feels bad about their clothes. Getting ready in the morning is quick, too. Priya says: My school doesn't have uniforms. I think choosing our own clothes is better because it shows our personality and creativity. Also, uniforms can cost a lot, and they are not always comfortable." Why does Leo like uniforms? Because nobody feels bad about their clothes, and the mornings are quick. What can our clothes show, according to Priya? Our personality. Now, here is a fun question. Leo's school has uniforms. Is that a fact or an opinion? It's a fact, because we can check it. Uniforms are better than our own clothes. Is that a fact or an opinion? It's an opinion, because people think differently. Amara says, I see your point, Leo, but I like choosing my own clothes. Leo smiles and says, That's fine! We can think differently and still be friends. Olive says, Thank you both. You disagreed so politely! Now, phonics. Today's words end in ity, too. Personal becomes personality. Creative, drop the e, becomes creativity. Similar becomes similarity. Say the part before ity strongly. per-son-AL-i-ty, cre-a-TIV-i-ty, sim-i-LAR-i-ty. Next time, Amara asks the council a new question: should we have longer breaks?

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Should students wear uniforms? Today, Olive rings her bell, and Amara raises her hand. She says, At my school, break time is only ten minutes. That's not enough time to go outside and come back! Olive says, Thank you, Amara. Who has an opinion? Remember to give a reason. Haru raises his hand and says, I think we should have longer breaks because we need time to relax. Say it with me. I think we should have longer breaks because we need time to relax. Excellent! An opinion is stronger with a reason and an example. Haru adds, For example, we can play outside and talk with our friends. Then Priya says, I partly agree. But then school will finish later. Both ideas are fair. Olive gives everyone a short article from the Hall's newsletter. Let's read the article. "Do children need longer breaks? Some people say yes. After a good break, many children can concentrate better in class. Break time is also an important activity, because children make friends, solve small problems, and move their bodies. Other people worry about longer breaks. If breaks are longer, the school day may finish later, or there may be less time for lessons. One possibility is to keep the same timetable but add one long break at lunchtime." Why can children concentrate better? Because they had a good break. What is one possibility? One long break at lunchtime. Leo says, I like that idea. Kiko says, Me, too, but let's ask the teachers what they think. Olive smiles and says, Good listeners make good speakers! Now, phonics. Active, drop the e, add ity. Activity. Able changes ble to bil. Ability. Possible changes ble to bil, too. Possibility. Say the part before ity strongly. ac-TIV-i-ty, a-BIL-i-ty, pos-si-BIL-i-ty. Next time, Priya brings the results of a survey about school rules!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, I think we should have longer breaks because we need time to relax. Today, Priya stands in the middle of the circle with a big sheet of paper. She did a survey! She asked all twenty council children five questions about school rules. Of course, the survey has no names, so nobody had to share private information. Priya says, Here are the results. Most students want to choose their own seats. Say it with me. Most students want to choose their own seats. Great! Most means more than half. When we talk about numbers, we can also say, Fifteen out of twenty. Let's read Priya's survey results. "School Rules Survey. Twenty council children answered. Fifteen out of twenty want to choose their own seats in class. Twelve want longer breaks. Eight think students should wear uniforms, and twelve do not. Seventeen think phones should stay in our bags during lessons. Only a few students, just two, want more homework! Thank you for answering. Your answers help us understand each other." How many children want to choose their own seats? Fifteen out of twenty. How many want more homework? Only two. Leo laughs and says, I'm one of the two! I like homework because it helps me remember. Priya says, That's a fact I didn't know about you! Then Kiko raises her hand. lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Everyone should have a chance to try. Today, Olive brings a picture book from the Hall's library. She says, Sometimes we see someone being unkind. What can we do? Let's think about it together. First, Ms. Emma tells us three important things. Never fight, and never laugh along. Stand up for your friend with calm, kind words. And always tell a teacher or another adult right away. You can say, Stop it. That's not kind. Say it with me. Stop it. That's not kind. Well done! Say it calmly, not angrily. Let's read the story. "Tom loves drawing. One day, Mia picks up his picture and laughs. Your dog looks like a potato, she says, and she teases him in front of everyone. Tom looks down. His friend Sam stands up and says calmly, Stop it. That's not kind. Then Sam stands next to Tom and asks, Are you OK? I'll stay with you. Together, they tell their teacher right away. The next day, Mia comes to Tom and says, I'm sorry. I was wrong. Tom accepts her apology, and they draw a dog together." What does Sam say to Mia? Stop it. That's not kind. What does Mia do the next day? She says sorry. Priya says, I think telling a teacher is the most important part because adults can help. Amara says, I partly agree. Staying with Tom is important, too, because then he doesn't feel scared. Leo says, I like the ending. People can change. Olive nods and says, Different people can coexist when we are kind to each other. Now, phonics. Inter means between, or with each other. The internet is networks connected with each other. Co means together. A coworker works together with you. Coexist means live together. Next time, we will learn how to invite someone to join us at break time!

We go out to the Hall's garden with Ms. Emma and play a ball game with Leo and Amara. Then Kiko sees a new council child named Ken. He is sitting by himself on a bench, looking at a book. Kiko walks over with a smile. She says, Hi, Ken. Do you want to join us? Say it with me. Do you want to join us? Lovely! Ken looks up and says, Sure! Thank you for asking. Is anyone sitting by themselves? Walk over, smile, and say, Do you want to join us? Use their name if you know it. Some people may want quiet time, and that is OK, too. You can say, Maybe next time! lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Let's make our school a kind place. Our Kindness Campaign was a big success, and today the Children's Council meets again. Olive rings her little wooden bell. Ding! She says, Every voice matters! Today, let's talk about something very important: children's rights. A right is something that every child should have, wherever they live. A long time ago, in 1989, many countries agreed on a list of children's rights. For example, children have the right to go to school. They have the right to play and rest. Leo grins and says, So soccer is a right! Everyone laughs, even Olive. Children have the right to learn and play. Say it with me. Children have the right to learn and play. Great! Olive points to a big poster on the wall. Let's read the poster. "Every child has rights. You have the right to learn, so you can go to school and ask questions. You have the right to play and rest, because your body and mind need time to grow. You have the right to be safe and healthy. You have the right to say what you think and be listened to. These rights are for every child, everywhere. And with rights come responsibilities, too." Why do children need to play and rest? Because their body and mind need time to grow. Who are these rights for? Every child, everywhere. Priya raises her hand and asks, What do you mean by responsibilities? Olive smiles. A responsibility is something you should do, like listening to others. Now, phonics. When we compare two things or correct someone, we say the new word strongly. Do you like that one? No, I like THIS one. Did you say Tuesday? No, I said THURSDAY. Should we meet at three? No, let's meet at FOUR. Is the library on the left? No, it's on the RIGHT. Next time, Amara will tell us all about her dog and her cat!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Children have the right to learn and play. Today, Amara brings her drawing book to the Children's Council. She loves animals, and she has drawn her two pets. Biscuit is a fluffy brown dog with floppy ears, and Pepper is a sleepy gray cat. Amara says, I love them so much, but having pets is not only fun. It's also a big job. Olive nods. That's a responsibility! When we have pets, we have to feed them, give them water, and keep them healthy. We are responsible for taking care of our pets. Say it with me. We are responsible for taking care of our pets. Excellent! Amara shows us the pet care chart from her kitchen wall. Let's read the chart. "Biscuit and Pepper's Care Chart. Morning: Amara walks Biscuit with Dad and fills both water bowls. Evening: Amara feeds Pepper, and her brother feeds Biscuit. Every Saturday: we brush Biscuit's fur and clean Pepper's bed. When a pet looks sick, we tell an adult, and we visit the vet together. Pets can't talk, so we watch them carefully. A happy pet needs food, water, exercise, and lots of love." Who feeds Pepper? Amara does. What do they do when a pet looks sick? They tell an adult and visit the vet together. Then Leo asks a question. Should children walk the dog every day? Haru thinks so, because dogs need exercise. Riko partly agrees. She says an adult should come, too, because the roads can be busy. Now, phonics. Remember, when we correct someone, the new word is strong. Do you feed the cat? No, I feed the DOG. Does Haru feed the fish? No, KIKO feeds the fish. Do you walk the dog at night? No, I walk him in the MORNING. Is the bowl empty? No, the bowl is FULL. Next time, let's talk about our jobs at home!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, We are responsible for taking care of our pets. Today, Olive asks the council a new question. What jobs do you do at home? These jobs are called chores. Leo says, I take out the trash bags. Amara says, I fold the laundry. Kiko says, I set the table, and I'm responsible for washing the dishes. Say it with me. I'm responsible for washing the dishes. Super! Priya laughs and says, In my family, we have a chore chart, so everyone knows their job. She shows us a photo of it. Let's read Priya's chore chart. "The Family Team Chart. Mom cooks dinner on weekdays, and Dad cooks on weekends. Priya is responsible for setting the table and feeding the fish. Her little brother puts the spoons away. Priya's big sister helps Mom cook, and Grandpa waters the plants. Every Saturday morning, we clean the house together and play music. When everyone helps a little, nobody is too tired, and we have more time for games." Who cooks dinner on weekends? Dad does. When does the family clean the house? Every Saturday morning. Then Olive asks, Should children help at home every day? Riko says yes, because a family is a team. Haru partly agrees. He thinks small jobs are enough on busy school days, because children also need time for homework and play. Olive rings her bell. Ding! Both of you gave good reasons! Now, phonics. Let's practice the strong new word again. Do you wash the dishes? No, I DRY the dishes. Does your brother cook? No, my SISTER cooks. Do you clean on Sunday? No, we clean on SATURDAY. Are you making lunch? No, I'm making DINNER. Next time, we will think about what children can do for Willowford, our community!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, I'm responsible for washing the dishes. We help our families at home. But what about our town? Today, Olive takes us to the big window of the Hall of Wisdom. We can see all of Willowford: little red roofs, a library with a clock, and the green trees of Willowford Park. Olive says, This town is a community. A community is all the people who live and work in a place. What can children do for our community? Say it with me. What can children do for our community? Wonderful! Leo says, We can say hello to our neighbors. It's easy, and it makes people smile. Priya says, We can help at the library and put the books back on the shelves. Then Ms. Emma finds a notice on the board by the door. Let's read the notice. "Willowford Park Clean-Up Day. Join us on Saturday afternoon from one to three! Bring a hat and a water bottle. We will give you gloves, tongs, and bags. Children must come with an adult. Last spring, our volunteers picked up forty bags of litter and planted sunflowers near the pond. Let's make our park clean and beautiful again. Thank you, Willowford!" When is the clean-up? On Saturday afternoon, from one to three. What did the volunteers plant last spring? Sunflowers. Kiko says, Why don't we join the clean-up? Ms. Emma says, Good idea, but we'll all go together with the adults. Now, phonics. Listen to the strong new words. Did you plant roses? No, we planted SUNFLOWERS. Is the event on Saturday morning? No, it's on Saturday AFTERNOON. Do you want the big poster? No, I want the SMALL poster. Is the station near the school? No, it's near the LIBRARY. Next time, we will give a talk about rights and responsibilities!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, What can children do for our community? On Saturday afternoon, we cleaned Willowford Park with Ms. Emma and the other adults, and we said hello to so many neighbors. Today is a special day. Each group will give a short talk about rights and responsibilities. Priya interviews Leo about safety at school. Amara talks about her pets. Then it's our turn. Riko stands up and says, I'd like to talk about rights and responsibilities. Olive says, Go ahead. We're listening. Riko's big idea is this. We have the right to speak, and we should listen to others. Say it with me. We have the right to speak, and we should listen to others. Beautiful! Let's read Riko's speech. "Hello, everyone. Children have many rights. We have the right to learn, so we should try our best at school. We have the right to play, so we should share the ball and take turns. We have the right to be safe, so we should help keep our town clean and safe. And we have the right to speak, and we should listen to others. Every voice matters, so every ear matters, too. Thank you!" What should we do because we have the right to play? Share the ball and take turns. Why does every ear matter? Because every voice matters. The audience claps, and Olive rings her bell. Then the Tree of Voices begins to glow. A third golden leaf slowly grows on its branch! Now, phonics. Let's review. Do you like that one? No, I like THIS one. Interview. Inter means each other, so you see each other and talk. Coexist. Co means together, so coexist means live together. Security. Secure, drop the e, and add ity. Say it strongly, se-CU-ri-ty. Next time, a very special visitor from the town is coming to the Hall of Wisdom!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, How about making a map for visitors? Today, Olive takes us outside, with Ms. Emma, to the empty lot next to the Hall of Wisdom. It's just dirt and a few old stones now, and the old fence needs to be repaired. Mayor Hart wants to know what the children would like here. Leo says, I think it should be a playground, because children need a place to run and play. Amara says, I see your point, but I think it should be a flower garden. Flowers make people happy, and bees need them, too. Leo and Amara are both right, so what can we do? Olive says, When two people want different things, we can look for a compromise（だきょうあん）. A compromise is an idea where both sides get some of what they want. Let's find a compromise. Say it with me. Let's find a compromise. Great job! Let's read Olive's notes on the board. "The Empty Lot. Leo's idea: a playground. Good points: children can run, climb, and play together. Amara's idea: a flower garden. Good points: it is beautiful, quiet, and good for bees. Our compromise: perhaps we can use both halves of the lot. A flower garden on one side and a small playground on the other side. It will require some benches and a path in the middle, so families can enjoy both." What is good about a flower garden? It is beautiful, quiet, and good for bees. What will be in the middle? Some benches and a path. Kiko says, What if we make a flower garden with a small playground? Leo and Amara smile. That sounds fair! Now, phonics. Maybe becomes perhaps. Need becomes require. A lot of plastic waste ends up in the sea, and it can hurt sea animals like turtles and seabirds. Here are three easy ideas. Bring your own bottle and fill it with water. Carry a reusable bag when you go shopping. Say no, thank you, to straws you don't need. Small steps can make a big difference!" How long can plastic take to break down? Hundreds of years. Which animals can plastic hurt? Sea animals, like turtles and seabirds. Then Haru says, I partly agree. Reusable bottles are great, but sometimes I forget mine. Riko says, I see your point. lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, I suggest that we bring our own bottles. This morning, almost everyone came with their own bottle! Ms. Emma says, Stage 4 is almost over. The graph shows that our class used less plastic this month. Wonderful! Kiko adds, It went down from one hundred twenty to forty. Leo says, That's a big difference! Let's read the report under the graph. "Plastic Bottles at the Hall of Wisdom. Last month, the Children's Council used one hundred twenty plastic bottles. This month, we used only forty. That is two thirds less! Most members now bring their own bottles. The recycling bin is next to the kitchen door, and the water fountain is to the right of the stairs, so please fill your bottle there. Let's keep going and make the next bar even shorter!" Children is the formal word for kids. Interrupt means to break in, so please don't interrupt. Suddenly, Birimo's old sea map glows blue. Our next adventure is under the sea! Goodbye, Olive!
